item.stem: Growing cells use phospholipids to build membranes and nucleic acids to store and transmit genetic information. The cells have enough of every required element except phosphorus. Which statement best explains how this shortage limits the production of these molecules?

choices.choice_text: Production of both phospholipids and nucleic acids is limited because both contain phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is a required component of both phospholipids and nucleic acids. A phosphorus shortage therefore limits the cells’ ability to build membranes and produce molecules that carry genetic information.

choices.choice_text: Only nucleic acid production is limited because phospholipids do not contain phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Trap: Overlooking phosphorus in phospholipids. Phospholipids also contain phosphorus, so their production is limited by the shortage. Fix: Check the required elements in both molecule types before predicting which production is limited.

choices.choice_text: Only phospholipid production is limited because nucleic acids require nitrogen instead of phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Trap: Treating nitrogen and phosphorus requirements as mutually exclusive. Nucleic acids contain both elements; having enough nitrogen does not remove their phosphorus requirement. Fix: Check whether a molecule requires multiple elements rather than choosing just one.

choices.choice_text: Neither type of molecule is affected because biological molecules require only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
choices.rationale: Trap: Confusing the most prevalent elements with the only required elements. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are abundant in biological molecules, but phospholipids and nucleic acids also require phosphorus. Fix: Identify each molecule’s required elements, not just the most abundant elements in living systems.

item.stem: A researcher asks whether phosphorus availability limits cells’ production of DNA, which stores hereditary information. Cells can be grown in media with controlled supplies of each element. All groups start with equal numbers of identical cells and are maintained at the same temperature for the same time. Which experimental design best tests the researcher’s question?

choices.choice_text: Compare DNA production in nitrogen-free and nitrogen-containing media, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts.
choices.rationale: Wrong-element trap: Nitrogen is also a component of DNA, but this comparison tests nitrogen availability rather than phosphorus availability. Fix: Match the manipulated element to the element named in the research question.

choices.choice_text: Compare DNA production in media lacking both phosphorus and nitrogen with media containing both, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts.
choices.rationale: Confounded-variables trap: Changing phosphorus and nitrogen together prevents attributing a difference in DNA production specifically to phosphorus. Either element could limit DNA production. Fix: Change phosphorus alone while keeping nitrogen and all other elements equally available.

choices.choice_text: Compare DNA production in phosphorus-free and phosphorus-containing media, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is a component of DNA, so its availability can limit production of this information-storing molecule. Changing only phosphorus availability and measuring DNA production directly tests the proposed relationship.

choices.choice_text: Compare phosphorus-free and phosphorus-containing media, keeping all other elements equally available in adequate amounts, and measure only phosphorus remaining in each medium.
choices.rationale: Dependent-variable mismatch: Measuring phosphorus remaining describes the medium, not how much DNA the cells produce. This measurement cannot establish whether phosphorus availability limits DNA production. Fix: Measure DNA production as the response to changing phosphorus availability.

item.stem: A laboratory produces nucleic acids that carry genetic information and phospholipids used in membranes. Two production batches have sufficient carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and sulfur, but shortages of nitrogen and phosphorus. Batch 1 receives enough nitrogen to eliminate its nitrogen shortage. Batch 2 receives enough nitrogen and phosphorus to eliminate both shortages. Neither batch has another source of either missing element, and no other factor limits production. How should production of the two materials compare between batches?

choices.choice_text: Both materials remain limited in batch 1, whereas both can reach normal production levels in batch 2.
choices.rationale: Nucleic acids need nitrogen and phosphorus, and phospholipids also need phosphorus. Batch 1 still lacks sufficient phosphorus for either material; batch 2 supplies both missing elements, removing the stated limitations.

item.stem: A nursery grows duckweed, a small aquatic plant, in nutrient solutions. Duckweed uses nucleic acids for genetic information and phospholipids for membranes. One group initially receives too little nitrogen and phosphorus, while all other required elements are sufficient. A first fertilizer treatment eliminates the nitrogen shortage but supplies no phosphorus. A second treatment then restores phosphorus to a sufficient level. Assuming these shortages are the only limits on production and the plants have no other phosphorus source, how will the second treatment affect nucleic acid and phospholipid production?

choices.choice_text: Only phospholipid production will recover because nucleic acid production already recovered when nitrogen became sufficient.
choices.rationale: Nitrogen-only nucleic acid trap: This treats nitrogen as the only missing element needed for nucleic acids. Their phosphorus requirement kept production limited after the first treatment, so the second treatment supports their recovery too. Fix: Check both nitrogen and phosphorus availability before predicting nucleic acid recovery.

choices.choice_text: Only nucleic acid production will recover because phospholipid production was already supported by sufficient carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
choices.rationale: All-lipids-are-alike trap: This incorrectly applies the elemental composition of fats to phospholipids. Phospholipids also contain phosphorus, so their production remained limited until the second treatment. Fix: Identify the lipid type and check whether it contains phosphorus.

choices.choice_text: Neither production rate will change because nitrogen from the first treatment already replaced phosphorus in both materials.
choices.rationale: Element-substitution trap: This assumes one abundant element can replace a different required element. Nitrogen cannot substitute for phosphorus in nucleic acids or phospholipids, so the first treatment left both phosphorus-limited. Fix: Match each shortage to the specific element supplied by the treatment.

choices.choice_text: Production of both materials can return to normal because the second treatment supplies an element required by both.
choices.rationale: Both nucleic acids and phospholipids contain phosphorus, so both remain limited after the nitrogen treatment. Supplying phosphorus removes the remaining elemental shortage, allowing normal production of both materials.

item.stem: An algae-production facility changes the nutrient mixture supplied to its cultures. The original mixture provided adequate amounts of every required element; the replacement supplies twice as much nitrogen but too little phosphorus, with all other required elements still adequate. The algae make nucleic acids for genetic information and phospholipids for membranes. After stored phosphorus is exhausted, and with no other phosphorus source, how should production of these materials compare with production before the change?

choices.choice_text: Production of both materials decreases because the phosphorus shortage restricts construction of both nucleic acids and phospholipids.
choices.rationale: Phosphorus is a required building material for both nucleic acids and phospholipids. Although nitrogen remains abundant, the reduced phosphorus supply prevents the algae from maintaining their previous production rates for either material.

choices.choice_text: Nucleic acid production stays at its previous rate because nitrogen is sufficient, while phospholipid production decreases because phosphorus is scarce.
choices.rationale: Nitrogen-only nucleic acid trap: This treats sufficient nitrogen as sufficient material for making nucleic acids. Their production also requires phosphorus, which is now limiting. Fix: Check for both nitrogen and phosphorus before predicting unchanged nucleic acid production.

choices.choice_text: Phospholipid production stays at its previous rate because carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are sufficient, while nucleic acid production decreases.
choices.rationale: All-lipids-are-alike trap: This overlooks the phosphorus requirement of phospholipids by treating all lipids as containing only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Those abundant elements cannot supply the missing phosphorus. Fix: Identify the lipid subtype and check its required elements.

choices.choice_text: Production of both materials stays at its previous rate because the extra nitrogen substitutes for the missing phosphorus.
choices.rationale: Element-substitution trap: This assumes an excess of one element can compensate for a shortage of another. Nitrogen cannot replace the phosphorus required in nucleic acids or phospholipids. Fix: Match each shortage to its required element rather than adding nutrient supplies together.
